2022 · arXiv · Benchmarks & Evals

News Summarization and Evaluation in the Era of GPT-3

On 100 recent CNN articles and 100 recent BBC articles, human annotators preferred zero-shot GPT-3 summaries over a fine-tuned state-of-the-art model and a multitask instruction-tuned model by at least 20 percentage points — while on the standard test splits, GPT-3's ROUGE-L score trailed the best available fine-tuned baseline by 6.7 to 20.4 points across all four benchmark datasets. The paper reads that gap as an indictment of the evaluation stack, not a straightforward model win.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Text summarization research had spent five years converging on one recipe: fine-tune a pre-trained language model on a large collection of article-summary pairs scraped from news sources — CNN/DailyMail's bullet points (Hermann et al., 2015), XSum's first-sentence-as-summary (Narayan et al., 2018), Newsroom's diverse extractive strategies (Grusky et al., 2018) — and then score the result against those same references with ROUGE, BERTScore, or a purpose-built factuality metric. GPT-3-style zero-/few-shot prompting had already reshuffled other NLP tasks, but the paper argues it had "only been studied for text summarization with unreliable automatic metrics" or in non-standard settings — nobody had put a prompted, non-fine-tuned model through the field's actual human-evaluation machinery and asked whether people, not metrics, still preferred the fine-tuned incumbents.

That question matters because the entire measurement apparatus — the reference summaries and the automatic metrics scored against them — was built and validated exclusively on fine-tuned systems that were trained to imitate those references. A model that generates good summaries without ever seeing them is exactly the case that apparatus was never tested against. If prompting turns out to produce summaries humans like better, but the metrics and gold standards say otherwise, that's not just a new best model — it's a sign the field's yardstick was measuring imitation of a specific (and, this paper argues, sometimes low-quality) reference style rather than summary quality itself.

// how it works

The method

The paper runs three systems head to head, chosen to span the space between full fine-tuning and pure prompting (Figure 2): BRIO (Liu et al., 2022), a task-specific model that reports state-of-the-art results after fine-tuning separately on CNN/DM and on XSum; T0 (Sanh et al., 2022) — 11B parameters per its own paper, a figure this paper never states itself — instruction-tuned on many tasks including summarization on those same datasets, a middle point between dataset-specific fine-tuning and a big generalist; and GPT3-D2, OpenAI's Instruct-series text-davinci-002, a 175B model — the one parameter count this paper does report — used purely zero-shot, with no fine-tuning and no in-context examples.

Fine-tuned models inherit the "style" of their training references, so to keep the comparison fair, GPT3-D2 is steered with nothing more than a natural-language sentence-count instruction — "Summarize the above article in N sentences" — with N set per dataset (3 for CNN/DailyMail, 2 for Newsroom, 1 for XSum/BBC) to match each dataset's reference length. The paper reports GPT3-D2 honored that length constraint in 98% of the human-study instances, with no other style control attempted.

Because GPT3-D2's pre-training and instruction-tuning data are undisclosed, the standard CNN/DM and XSum test splits are contamination risks for the human study specifically — GPT3-D2 could simply have memorized their reference summaries. So the human evaluation runs on fresh data: 100 CNN articles and 100 BBC articles collected between March and June 2022 ("CNN-2022" and "BBC-2022"), chosen specifically to reduce the chance GPT3-D2 had already seen them — though the paper is explicit elsewhere that it doesn't actually know GPT3-D2's training cutoff or data. Annotators, recruited through Prolific and paid roughly $11/hr, are shown all three systems' summaries for a given article in an A/B design with no quality definitions supplied (to avoid imposing the authors' own notion of "good"), and mark their most- and least-preferred summary or summaries, with free-text rationales. 60 unique annotators per dataset each rate 5 articles, and each article is rated by 3 annotators — 300 judgments per dataset. To keep the comparison honest, the authors also patch a known failure mode of BRIO-XSum (it was trained on a version of XSum with the first sentence stripped out, so roughly 30% of its outputs on full articles are low quality): they either pick a cleaner candidate from a beam of 10 or, failing that, feed BRIO-XSum the article with its first sentence removed to match its training distribution — a step taken specifically to keep the baseline fair, not to weaken it, though the paper itself notes this fallback "often results in factually incorrect summary generations."

A second study, run separately, scores the same three systems plus PEGASUS — a fourth fine-tuned baseline reported on all four datasets, added specifically because BRIO fine-tuned models aren't available for every dataset — with automatic metrics on 500 articles randomly sampled from the standard test split of each of the four benchmark datasets — a different, older evaluation set than the human study's fresh 2022 articles, chosen for statistical power at a fixed API budget (the paper cites Card et al., 2020, on power analysis). The metric suite spans reference-based overlap metrics (ROUGE, METEOR, BLEU), reference-based similarity metrics (BERTScore, MoverScore), a reference-based QA metric (QAEval), and reference-free quality/factuality metrics (SUPERT, BLANC, QuestEval, QAFactEval, FactCC, DAE, SummaC).

// what they found

The results

On both datasets, GPT3-D2 wins the majority-vote "best summary" count by a wide margin, and the gap is statistically significant (paired bootstrap, CNN p = 2×10⁻³, BBC p = 6×10⁻⁴):

DatasetBRIO best↑/worst↓T0 best↑/worst↓GPT3-D2 best↑/worst↓
CNN36 / 248 / 6758 / 9
BBC20 / 5630 / 2957 / 15

GPT3-D2 beats the next-best system by 22 points on CNN (over BRIO) and 27 points on BBC (over T0). But the margin is a majority-vote effect, not a consensus one: Krippendorff's α with MASI distance — a chance-corrected reliability coefficient, not a raw agreement rate — comes out low: 0.05 (CNN best) and 0.11 (CNN worst), 0.18 (BBC best) and 0.15 (BBC worst). The paper's own read: GPT3-D2's preference is unanimous across all three annotators for fewer than 30% of articles, while BRIO or T0 still receive at least one "best" vote on more than 60% of articles (Figure 5).

Automatic metrics tell the opposite story. On reference-based metrics (Table 4 in the paper), GPT3-D2's ROUGE-L trails the best available fine-tuned model by 6.7 points on CNN, 11.1 on DailyMail, 20.4 on XSum, and 13.5 on Newsroom (against PEGASUS, the only fine-tuned baseline available there) — a wider range than the paper's own headline framing of "7 ROUGE-L points on average" (§4.1 elsewhere frames it as ">7 ROUGE-L points between GPT3-D2 and BRIO," a narrower comparison than the four-dataset spread above). T0 matches or outscores GPT3-D2 on ROUGE-L/METEOR/BLEU/BERTScore across CNN, DailyMail and XSum (11 of those 12 comparisons strictly favor T0, with an exact tie on CNN's METEOR score, .25 vs .25) — flipping only on Newsroom, the one dataset T0 wasn't trained on, where GPT3-D2 outscores T0 on all four of those metrics (even as it still trails PEGASUS on ROUGE-L there, per the 13.5-point gap above). Reference-free metrics don't rescue the human ranking either (Table 5): the two "Overall Quality" metrics, SUPERT and BLANC, rank GPT3-D2 below BRIO on CNN and DailyMail (matching the reference-based direction) but above it on XSum. The factuality metrics disagree even with each other — on CNN, FactCC scores GPT3-D2 highest of the three systems (.2428) while DAE scores it lowest (.6671, versus BRIO's .7577) — and the two only agree on XSum, where both put GPT3-D2 clearly ahead of the fine-tuned baselines.

The advantage extends, qualitatively, beyond generic summarization. In a keyword-focused human study (same 100 CNN articles, two named-entity keywords per article, GPT3-D2 vs. the fine-tuned CTRLSum baseline), annotators preferred GPT3-D2 by majority vote 69.8% of the time to CTRLSum's 30.2% (Figure 7). Aspect-based summarization — mapping a query like "who is the defendant or under trial?" onto the article — gets no human study at all, only worked examples (Figure 6), and the results are explicitly "mixed": in one example, asked who is a defendant or under investigation, GPT3-D2 answers "Donald Trump. The FBI. The Department of Justice. Sandy Berger" — four entities, two of them institutions, not the single defendant the article actually names.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The human-preference result is real and the metric-disagreement result is real — both are checkable directly from the paper's own tables, and they hold up under re-derivation. What's less settled is how much weight the paper's framing — prompting beats fine-tuning, and the metrics are broken — can bear versus a narrower, more defensible reading.

Start with scale, which the paper never quantifies across its three systems. GPT3-D2 is 175B parameters — the one size this paper states. T0 is 11B and BRIO fine-tunes a sub-billion-parameter backbone (BART for CNN/DM, PEGASUS for XSum), both per their own papers (Sanh et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022) — Goyal et al. report neither number. The paper's Limitations section runs three paragraphs — no standardized task design for human evaluation (A/B vs. Likert-scale vs. multi-dimension ratings), English-news-only generalization, and GPT3-D2's undisclosed RLHF/instruction-tuning data (a confound the authors partly wave off themselves: "our arguments in this paper do not rely on the specifics of the GPT3-D2 system, merely that such a system exists") — but never raises model size. A reader can't tell from this paper alone whether people are rewarding zero-shot prompting as a paradigm, or simply a much larger, more fluent language model — the comparison is prompting-vs-fine-tuning and small-vs-large-model at the same time, and the paper doesn't separate them.

There's a baseline-fairness wrinkle in the human study too. BRIO-XSum's repair for its known bad-training-data problem — resampling with the article's first sentence stripped when the beam of 10 doesn't turn up a clean candidate — is something the paper itself flags as often producing factually incorrect summaries. On BBC, annotators' most common stated reason for rating BRIO the worst summary was exactly "misleading or incorrect information." The repair is a legitimate attempt to match BRIO's training distribution, but it may also be quietly manufacturing part of the very failure mode that cost BRIO the BBC vote.

Contamination is handled asymmetrically. The human study deliberately uses fresh March–June 2022 articles specifically to dodge GPT3-D2 memorizing CNN/DM or XSum's test-set references — a real methodological care point. But the metrics study, which is where the paper's central automatic-metric-unreliability claim comes from, runs on the standard pre-2020 test splits GPT3-D2 may well have seen during training; the paper's own footnote admits the overlap risk and dismisses it with "we do not observe a qualitative difference in GPT3-D2's performance on these older articles" — an anecdotal check, not a quantified one, for exactly the claim (automatic-metric unreliability) that most needs it ruled out.

The "best summary" vote is also a coarser instrument than the conclusion drawn from it. It's a single omnibus preference judgment with no separate fluency, coherence, or factuality question — annotators were told to "carefully check factuality" but that's folded into one vote, not scored on its own — and, as shown above, Krippendorff's α for these votes is low (0.05–0.18) while unanimous three-way agreement on GPT3-D2 holds for fewer than 30% of articles. The paper is candid about this (it says so directly, twice), but a headline stated as "GPT3-D2 outperforms the next best model by at least 20 percentage points" reads more confidently than the underlying annotator-level signal supports.

The paper does run one relevant check: GPT3-D2 summaries are about 9 words longer in total than BRIO's on CNN (Appendix B; Table 2 separately shows GPT3-D2 averaging 23.4 words/sentence to BRIO's 15.8), so its preference edge could in principle be a length effect. Plotting, per article, the difference in summary length against the difference in annotator votes between GPT3-D2 and the next-best system (Figure 8), the paper reports low correlation — Pearson's ρ = 0.17 for CNN and 0.02 for BBC — and concludes that "these correlation values cannot solely explain the large differences in annotator judgments." That's a real, checkable robustness pass the paper ran on itself, but its own hedge is that length isn't the whole story, not that it's ruled out.

baselines

T0 (11B, per Sanh et al. 2022) and BRIO (a sub-billion-parameter BART/PEGASUS backbone, per Liu et al. 2022) are both far smaller than the 175B GPT3-D2 — neither of those two sizes comes from Goyal et al. themselves; the paper reports no size-matched fine-tuned or instruction-tuned comparison, so the paradigm claim and a plain scale claim are entangled and untested against each other.

contamination

Rigorously avoided for the human study (fresh 2022 articles); waved off with an anecdotal check for the metrics study, which runs on the pre-2020 standard test splits GPT3-D2 may have trained on.

what's missed

A single best/worst vote stands in for quality; the paper's own agreement numbers (α = 0.05–0.18) show individual annotators frequently disagree even where the majority vote is lopsided. Aspect-based summarization — half of the paper's third research question, alongside keyword-focused summarization, which does get a human study — has no human evaluation at all.

would raise confidence

Disclosure (or a proxy estimate) of GPT3-D2's fine-tuning/RLHF data; a size-controlled instruction-tuned baseline; per-dimension human ratings (fluency, coherence, factuality) instead of one omnibus vote; a quantified contamination check on the metrics-study test splits.

// bottom line

The strongest, most defensible version of this paper's contribution isn't that GPT-3 is simply a better summarizer than BRIO — it's that the evaluation apparatus built for fine-tuned summarization (gold references scraped from news sites, plus metrics trained or tuned against fine-tuned systems' error profiles) stops tracking human preference the moment a genuinely different generation process enters the comparison. That's a real and checkable finding. Whether it's specifically prompting that broke the metrics, versus a much bigger model, versus RLHF-style training the paper can't inspect, is left open by the paper's own design.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. On fresh 2022 CNN and BBC articles, human annotators majority-vote preferred zero-shot GPT3-D2 (text-davinci-002) over fine-tuned BRIO and instruction-tuned T0 by 22 and 27 percentage points respectively — while GPT3-D2's ROUGE-L score trails the best available fine-tuned baseline (BRIO where trained, PEGASUS on Newsroom) by 6.7–20.4 points on the standard test splits.
  2. Reference-free metrics don't recover the human ranking either: the two quality metrics (SUPERT, BLANC) track the reference-based direction on CNN/DailyMail but flip on XSum, and the factuality metrics (FactCC vs. DAE) disagree with each other about GPT3-D2 everywhere except XSum, where both agree it scores highest.
  3. The preference generalizes to keyword-focused summarization (69.8% win rate over CTRLSum) — the human-evaluated half of the paper's third research question, "how can prompting be used beyond generic summarization?" The other half, aspect-based summarization, gets no human study at all — only qualitative examples with "mixed" results, including a documented factual error.
  4. The human-preference margin is a majority-vote effect sitting on weak per-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's α 0.05–0.18) — the paper reports this itself and it tempers how "clear" the preference really is at the individual level.
  5. Model scale (175B GPT3-D2 vs. 11B T0 vs. BRIO's sub-billion-parameter backbone — the last two per their own papers, not Goyal et al.'s) and the metrics study's use of pre-2020, potentially-contaminated test splits are two confounds the paper doesn't fully rule out — worth keeping in mind before reading this as a clean prompting-beats-fine-tuning result rather than a case study in the evaluation stack breaking down when a different kind of model shows up.
